outcome: A preprint by Cembrano, Fischer and Klimm (arXiv:2604.02058, first posted 2 April 2026, revised 2 August 2026) constructs an explicit symmetric strategy ('FSD') that strictly beats the Anderson–Weber strategy for every n≥4 in the symmetric rendezvous search problem on n discrete locations, thereby settling — in the negative — the 1990 Anderson–Weber conjecture that their strategy is optimal for all n (the conjecture had already been confirmed for n=2,3 by Weber in 2012, and disproved specifically for n=4 by an earlier, pre-2024 paper). No expert digestion, journal acceptance, or independent verification beyond an AI-assisted 'Pith Review' has been found.

counterexample.object: An explicit symmetric strategy ('First-Same-or-Different', FSD) for n≥4 locations, correlating consecutive tours of non-home locations via a derangement-graph construction, whose expected meeting time is strictly smaller than that of the Anderson–Weber strategy for every n≥4.
counterexample.verified_how: Explicit construction with closed-form/asymptotic bounds on the improvement (e.g. an explicit ~0.00125 reduction for n=4, and an explicit lower bound on the improvement of order (n−1)⁻⁸ for n≥5); an independent (AI-assisted) review flagged one hand-checked monotonicity step (Lemma 11, covering n≥8) as the main point not fully automated/formally verified.

summary: The Wikipedia bullet 'Rendezvous problem' links only to the general Rendezvous problem article, which (per the frozen January 2024 wording as fetched) covers several distinct sub-problems: the continuous 'telephone problem' rendezvous value on the line (bounds ~4.152–4.257, still open and untouched), and the discrete symmetric rendezvous game on n locations, where Anderson and Weber conjectured in 1990 that their round-based strategy is optimal for all n. That conjecture was confirmed for n=2,3 by Weber (2012, pre-window) and known to fail for n=4 specifically from an earlier paper (arXiv:0912.0670, 2009, pre-window). Since the January 2024 freeze, Cembrano, Fischer and Klimm posted 'Faster Symmetric Rendezvous on Four or More Locations' (arXiv:2604.02058, v1 2 April 2026, v2 2 August 2026), which generalizes the n=4 counterexample into an explicit strategy beating Anderson–Weber for *every* n≥4, closing the conjecture in full (negatively) modulo one hand-checked monotonicity lemma noted by an automated/AI-assisted review site ('Pith Review'). I treat this as within scope: the Wikipedia article explicitly frames the Anderson–Weber conjecture and its resolution status as part of 'the rendezvous problem played in n discrete locations,' so a full resolution of that conjecture for n≥4 is a change to what a careful reader of this article's content would now write, even though the specific numeric-bound sub-question (rendezvous value on the line, distance 2) is untouched. I found no evidence of any AI system contributing to the mathematical content: no acknowledgement, methods section, or author statement mentions AI/ML tool use in deriving or checking the FSD strategy or its analysis; the only AI-related item found ('Pith Review') is a third-party AI-assisted review of the paper, not an input to the result, so ai_role is none. Because the live Wikipedia article (last modified 20 February 2025, per fetch) still only mentions the n=3 resolution and says nothing about n≥4, and I found no journal acceptance, no blog treatment by rendezvous-search specialists (e.g., Alpern, Weber), and only the AI-assisted Pith Review as external commentary, I classify this as claimed rather than resolved: no independent human expert digestion was located.
competing_reading: One could argue the n≥4 generalization is a 'related problem' relative to the specific bullet, since the Wikipedia bullet points only to the general article and the frozen revision's own text emphasizes the n=3 resolution and the line-search bounds as the flagship open sub-problems, with the general-n Anderson–Weber conjecture mentioned only implicitly via 'even the symmetric rendezvous problem played in n discrete locations... has turned out to be very difficult to solve.' Under a stricter reading limited to the numerically-bounded line problem (distance-2 rendezvous value, 4.152–4.257), status would instead be open/no_change_found, since no source found any movement on those bounds since January 2024. I resolved this by treating the whole article's content as the scope, per the instruction that a bullet linking only a general article still requires researching the problem's own name and full scope; the Anderson–Weber conjecture is explicitly named and tracked in that article as an unsolved (at the time) sub-problem of 'the rendezvous problem.'
what_would_settle_it: Confirmation of whether a human expert (e.g., a referee report, journal acceptance, or a specialist's blog/survey treatment) has independently verified the FSD construction and its Lemma 11 monotonicity step, which would upgrade the status from claimed to resolved; alternatively, an explicit statement from Wikipedia editors or the rendezvous-search community on whether they consider the n≥4 case now closed.

dead_ends: Distributed-computing 'rendezvous in labeled lines' work (arXiv:2505.04564) — a related but distinct deterministic-graph-rendezvous problem, not the symmetric search game or the line-bound problem; not in scope.

'Oblivious Self-Distance Symmetric Rendezvous on the Integer Line' (arXiv:2609.13632, Sept 2026) — a variant with an added memory/obliviousness restriction giving Θ(d²) time, a different (harder, restricted) model rather than a case or resolution of the classical symmetric rendezvous-on-the-line problem; treated as a related problem, not counted.
No movement found on the classical distance-2 symmetric rendezvous value on the line (still bounded in (4.1520, 4.2574) as of all sources checked).

judgement.doubts: The bullet is the whole 'Rendezvous problem', which also includes the continuous symmetric rendezvous value on the line (bounds ~4.152–4.257), untouched per the record. Settling the Anderson–Weber sub-conjecture for all n>=4 is therefore a case (F2), the exact example named in JUDGE.md. The Pith Review mention of Lemma 11 is an automated review and is neither digestion nor a knock-down (F11). The strategy is explicit, but its superiority for n>=5 rests on analytic bounds, not a simple direct check, so verification stays unreviewed; this does not affect the partial tier.
